-and that is the reason I like to give him some advice. At any rate, within a few days the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance will be sitting down in London with representatives from other parts of the commonwealth to discuss and consider the whole field of commonwealth trade and finance, and perhaps other relations. We sincerely hope that the government will exhibit at that conference a considerably changed attitude toward commonwealth relations and commonwealth trade from what we think they have been exhibiting most of the time since the war ended. The Liberal government has been altogether too tough in the matter of convertibility, and they have taken a line which has gradually diminished what our trade with the other parts of the commonwealth could have been if they had used more vision and determination to strengthen commonwealth trade rather than merely to follow the line of least resistance and the lead of the United States of America.
To be completely fair about the situation, it is true that during the war the pattern of trade had to change to some degree because at that time Britain could not supply Canada's needs, in the traditional manner, of the things we had to import. However, that is no excuse for letting the pattern continue as it has during the seven years since the war ended in 1945.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberals are just now beginning to wake up to the fact that they have hitched themselves to the most uncertain market in the world, the most uncertain market for Canada-that is the market in the United States; and for all too long they have neglected to do what ought to have been done to restore Canada to the best market she ever had and the market which she ought to continue to hold if she can in the years to come. I am speaking now, Mr. Speaker, entirely from the point of view of the good of Canada when I say we should serve the best interests of our own country and the commonwealth as a whole. I think the government should hang its head in shame over the fact that Britain has had to go behind the iron curtain, to Russia, to the enemy of the free world for a number of things she has had to get such as coarse grain, lumber, and things like that which Canada could very well have supplied.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is hindsight.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You can talk about hindsight but there ought to be just a little bit of vision and foresight as well.

I quite realize that since the war ended in 1945 Canada had advanced a grand total of $1,763,900,000 in financial assistance to other countries up to March 31 of this year. Of that figure $1,185 million represent loans to Great Britain, all of which will be recoverable in the future. In addition there were certain direct credits that were made available to some of the European countries. I will not detail those at the moment. In addition to those credits made available to certain European countries, contributions sent to the United Nations agencies have totalled $203,100,000, which includes $154 million advanced to UNRRA, $12 million to post-UNRRA relief, $15 million for the Colombo plan assistance to India, $10 million for assistance to Pakistan, and just over $1 million contributed by Canada to the technical co-operation payments plan for India, Pakistan, Ceylon, and Greece. Some $325 million has been contributed by Canada for military aid to NATO countries. That was very largely a transfer of existing stocks of armaments and equipment which the Canadian army had been keeping as a mobilization reserve. Actually every Canadian has contributed $46.40 in these forms of aid to other countries, which is not recoverable.
Now, sir, Britain has been the biggest beneficiary of the Canadian assistance I have outlined, and I am not pleading that we continue to help Britain in the ways I have cited and which have been the pattern since 1945. I think we must consider much greater aid to the underprivileged countries under the Colombo plan and the technical co-operation arrangements. I much prefer to see us drop sacks of wheat and food materials into these underprivileged countries to help them live in some measure of happiness and contentment, than to be draining off our production in the form of arms and shells to destroy our fellow men in warfare. In my judgment food can be made a far more effective weapon than atom bombs; and using that weapon, peace could be brought to this world much more quickly than by all the military campaigns that could ever be fought.
We think there are very worth while, physically and financially possible measures that can be taken by Canada to help these countries that are in need and to help Britain and other parts of the commonwealth get on their feet, particularly Britain. We have believed and asserted over the past seventeen years-and by "we" I mean the Social Credit group-that the British commonwealth of nations offers the only assurance of bringing balance once more into a world of trade that has become seriously out of balance. What the government seems to have forgotten is that our great neighbour to the south, the
The Address-Mr. Low United States of America, has within her borders as much as 50 per cent of the world's total industrial capacity. This makes her a colossus both in the industrial world and in the world of trade.
Ever since the United States became the industrial giant she is, she has had a tendency to hog the channels of trade and has consistently refused to balance her trade with the rest of the world. This has brought about a condition under which the other countries of the world have not been able to secure enough American dollars to be able to buy from the United States the things they needed. As a consequence the streams of trade have to quite a large degree been dried up; and perforce, the United States has had to resort to Marshall plans and gifts of great quantities of goods to other countries to make up for what normal trade ought to be doing.
If the British commonwealth of nations with its widely scattered territories, its tremendous production, and its very large population will revitalize their sinews into strong unity it can become the one factor which is capable of bringing order and balance into an unbalanced world of trade. Canada should be taking the lead in this revitalization. Thus far since the war the Liberal government of Canada has been very diffident in its approach to commonwealth matters and has been an abject follower, instead of the bold and courageous leader that everyone had the right to think it should be.
When the Canadian representatives sit down at the London conference they ought to be guided by the determination to restore our traditional trade patterns, and not worry their heads off about this business of convertibility of currencies. We in this group feel that every effort should be made by Britain and by us to help Britain once more get investments in other parts of the commonwealth. Britain should even now be doing something about investments in Canada. There is still ground floor space in such things as the petroleum industry where, specifically, I will name the Athabasca tar sands. If Britain will make a supreme effort she can get hold of a block of those sands and set out, like some of the other countries, to perfect methods of separation so that eventually she will contribute to her own and the world's supply of petroleum products. As I say, other countries are getting into it, and I think Canada should be doing everything possible to help Britain to get into the oil development in this country. In due time the investment will pay off handsomely. The thing is physically possible, and we Social Crediters have always claimed that what is physically possible can be made

The Address-Mr. Low financially possible. In the years ahead Britain will have to have returns in the form of investment income if she is to maintain her place in the world of commerce.
In the second place, Canada must be prepared to send to Britain the food materials and a good many other raw materials which Britain needs and which we can supply, not in the form of gifts or loans but on a straight deal. The Prime Minister used some words this afternoon and this evening which I thought were not very logical. He reminded us that Britain in the past year had bought something like $631 million worth of goods from us and that Canada, a nation of 14 million, had bought something over $400 million from Britain. There was a $200 million disparity. Britain cannot afford to buy $600 million worth of goods from Canada if we only buy $400 million from her. It is just impossible. Somehow the disparity has to be made up.
The Social Credit group in this house for a good many years has advocated that Canada should be prepared to accept from Britain in payment for these goods the only thing Britain has to pay with at the present time, namely her own currency, sterling. There is no doubt in my mind that Canada can trade about amongst the countries of the sterling area to obtain with the sterling the things which Canada needs. It may take a little time, but if in accepting sterling we help Britain to get on her feet, and at the same time sell to advantage the products which we have to export, it will be worth taking the time. And while we are trading around in the sterling area there is no question in my mind about the ability to finance the whole deal within Canada, just as in 1917 we financed the advance of wheat to Great Britain by an issue which was arranged by the minister of finance.
Canada should also show her good faith in this whole matter of the revitalization of the commonwealth by encouraging the import into this country of those things which Britain can supply. There are encouraging reports now coming out of Britain which indicate that since the socialist government was defeated production has gone ahead by leaps and bounds. Canada is going to need quantities of television material. I am convinced that the British product is the best in the world. There is no reason why Britain should not supply Canada's needs in this respect just as fast as Canada expands her television program.
That is not all. In the field of the development of the St. Lawrence system Britain could supply us with great quantities of steel headgates and materials that will be used to develop this waterway. We should be prepared to buy them from Britain. In my

judgment there is no reason why those things should not be done. In addition to that, we should encourage imports of other things that Britain could supply, including automobiles. I believe we should be ashamed of the fact that in Canada we hear a lot of criticism about the antiquated production methods of Britain, and charges that the cost of British goods has been made inordinately high as a consequence of the British social security system, while at the same time we put every obstacle in the way of marketing their automobiles in Canada. I say we ought to be ashamed of ourselves. We Canadians declare to the world that we believe in competition, yet we do everything we can to prevent competition. At least certain entrenched interests in this country do so, and they do it with the sanction and assistance of this government; at least that is the way it appears to me.
The situation is pretty well summed up, Mr. Speaker, in this editorial which was published not so long ago in the Calgary Herald. I am just going to quote briefly from it.
When the two big winter automobile shows are held next February, in Toronto and Montreal, the first major shows since the war, there will be no British cars on view before the Canadian public. They have been black-balled by the Canadian automobile industry.
When British motor manufacturers and traders revealed what was going on, and protested, the National Automobile Shows Inc. at first maintained utter silence, and then its general manager, J. L. Stewart, came up with the explanation that the exclusion of British cars was not a question of patriotism or of international economics, but was a simple matter of everyday business. Canadian firms, he said, had invested several million dollars in facilities and advertising, and they did not propose to invite companies outside the association to share the benefits of their advertising benefits.
He did not explain how it is that a number of United States firms which have not kicked in to the association since 1927 will be showing their cars.
He might also explain how it is that at the world-famous Earl's Court motor show in London, an immeasurably fancier and more expensive show than any Canadian association is apt to venture into, there is a distinct section set aside for the display of Canadian-made cars.
That is good sportsmanship, and I think we ought to be exhibiting the same kind of sportsmanship in this country. If we expect Britain to buy from us, we have to be prepared to buy from her and to do so on a competitive basis, not some arbitrary basis that some of these people like to think up.
I need not point out at any length, Mr. Speaker, that we have hitched ourselves to a very uncertain market, that is the one in the United States. Events of the past ten months should have served to convince a lot of foolish people that the United States of America does not need too many of the products which Canada produces. Whenever it

suits her purpose to do so, without any warning whatever, the United States is apt to throw up embargoes or tariffs to keep out Canadian production. The foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan gave her a perfect excuse for excluding Canadian meat products. There is no good reason in this world, except of course for the fact she does not need to import those products to Canada, why the embargo should have continued as long as it has. Our cheese was excluded from the United States last summer, and the consequences nearly ruined the cheese industry of central Canada. The United States seems to consider she is not bound by the Geneva trade agreement, although she would yell to high heaven if Canada were to exhibit such ideas and tendencies.
The Liberal government was very foolish and shortsighted to allow Canada to become dependent on these uncertain United States markets. As I said, I am not speaking from sentiment at all in this regard but from the necessity of restoring our traditional markets. It is largely from the sense of good business for Canada and Canadians, as well as from a well-founded belief that the British commonwealth, if it strengthens its ties and comes to a unity of purpose, will go far towards restoring balance and Christian decency in world trade. For seventeen years we Social Crediters have taken essentially this same position which, Mr. Speaker, gives the absolute lie to the statement that was made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) in my own constituency not so long ago when he attended a Liberal convention there. I wish he were in his seat right now, because I should like to talk to him pretty straight.
This is the same minister who, at the Liberal convention in Calgary, made the statement that if the government does not win the next election it will be because the government has been doing too good a job of statesmanship and not enough of playing politics. At the nominating convention in my constituency this self-styled statesman told the people that he believed Mr. Low's talk about empire ties and preferential tariffs for commonwealth countries was catering to British sentiment in Ontario. He said, "I don't think he is sincere."

Hear, hear.
The Address-Mr. Low

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I hear "hear, hear" from the member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). I am sure, of course, that the people of this country, of the Peace river country and of Alberta, cannot lose sight of the fact that in making that claim the minister from Edmonton, who claimed that I am not sincere-this goes for the member for Ottawa West as well if that is what he meant by his "hear, hear"-was definitely getting off the path of statesmanship and down into the gutter of very questionable politics. Now, I ask who are they-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I ask, who are they to deny anybody's sincerity?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps out of fairness to the hon. member I ought to say that I understood that in making the reference he did to the improvement in empire trade he was seeking to appeal to the British sentiment in Ontario; that was what I understood the quotation to be, and when he read the quotation I added the "hear, hear" because I agree.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wonder how long a man does have to keep pressing for the strengthening of the commonwealth and the restoration of our traditional market, that is the market the Liberals have thrown out the window, before he can convince the minister from Edmonton-there may be some others-that he is sincere. Certainly seventeen years ought to be sufficient. For seventeen years, Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit movement has been preaching the same doctrine, and it has not been for the mere purpose of catching votes in Ontario. We have taken that position because we sincerely believe it is the best way to build for peace and decency. It is also the best business for Canada.
It is now ten o'clock, sir, and I do not know what your desires are with respect to adjournment. I do have some time left, but if it is your desire I shall leave it until tomorrow.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is it the wish of the house that I call it ten o'clock?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.
